summary: John B. Cobb Jr. is a scholar of philosophy and religious studies who earned his PhD at the University of Chicago. He founded the Center for Process Studies and held professorships at Claremont School of Theology and Claremont Graduate University (attested 1989).

John Beames was an Indology and linguistics scholar. Educated at Merchant Taylors' School and East India Company College (Haileybury, 1856–1857), he served in the Indian Civil Service from around 1858 to 1893.

John Borthwick Gilchrist worked in linguistics and Indology, earning an LL.D. from Edinburgh. He served in the East India Company, headed Fort William College, taught at East India Company College, and became University College London's first Professor of Hindustani (c. 1828–1831).
John Bray works in Tibetology and history/archaeology. He studied under Tsering Dhundup Gonkatsang and has held a post at the International Association for Ladakh Studies.

John Briggs was an Indology and history/archaeology scholar who studied at Eton College until 1799. He served in the East India Company from around 1801 to 1835, succeeding James Cunningham Grant-Duff.

John Brockington is an Indologist who completed his M.A. and D.Phil. at the University of Oxford. He spent his career at the University of Edinburgh, serving as Senior Lecturer in Sanskrit (attested 1987) and later Emeritus Professor of Sanskrit (attested 1998–2003).

John Brough, an Indologist, linguist, and Buddhist studies scholar, studied under A. B. Keith at Edinburgh and H. W. Bailey at St John's College, Cambridge. He served as Professor of Sanskrit at SOAS (1948–1967) and Professor at Cambridge (1967–1984).
John Buescher works in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He completed his doctoral dissertation at the University of Virginia in 1982 and served as Director at Voice of America (attested 2001).
John Burnet was a scholar of philosophy who studied at Edinburgh and Balliol College, Oxford. He held a long-standing academic post at the University of St Andrews from around 1892 to 1926.

John Burton-Page was an Indologist, linguist, and historian. Educated at Oxford and Deccan College, he worked at Deccan College (c. 1958–1960) and served at SOAS University of London as Lecturer (1950) and Reader (1971–1982).
John C. Huntington was a scholar of history, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology. He served as a professor at Ohio State University (attested 1987–1990 and 2000).

John C. Maraldo is a scholar of philosophy, Buddhist studies, and Japanology. He held a post at the University of North Florida (attested 1988), where he became distinguished professor emeritus of philosophy (attested 2015).

John Campbell Oman was a scholar of Indology and religious studies. He worked for the Public Works Department (1866–1877), as Professor at Government College University, Lahore (1877–1897), and as Principal of Khalsa College (1898–1899).
John Capper worked in the fields of Indology and history/archaeology. He founded The Ceylon Magazine in 1840 and served as editor of the Ceylon Times from 1858 to 1874.
John Carnac Morris was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at the East India Company College from 1815 to 1817 and entered the Madras Civil Service in 1818.

John Caspar Leyden was an Indology and linguistics scholar. He studied at the University of Edinburgh from around 1790 to 1797 and was appointed professor of Hindustani at Fort William College in 1808.

John Chadwick was a linguist and historian. Educated at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, he worked on the Oxford Latin Dictionary (c. 1946–1952) and served as Perceval Maitland Laurence Reader in Classics at Cambridge (1969–1984).

John Clark Archer was a scholar of religious studies and Indology who completed his B.D., M.A., and Ph.D. at Yale University. He spent his career at Yale (1914–1950), becoming the Hocker Professor of Comparative Religion in 1932.
John Clark Marshman was an Indologist and historian. He founded Serampore College in 1818 and directed the affairs of the Serampore Mission beginning in 1819.

John Claude White worked in Tibetology and history/archaeology. He studied at Rugby School and the Royal Indian Engineering College (c. 1873–1876), then joined the Bengal Public Works Department as an Assistant Engineer in 1876.
